success_criteria.description: All three districts are in use and every precinct is assigned.
All three districts have roughly equal population (within 15%).

character.name: You
character.motivation: Three parties are on the ballot across the Bend: the Ken Party out west, the Ryu Party in the city, and the Chun-Li Party out east. Each runs a candidate in every district — but each is strongest on its home ground. Three bases, three corners. Where you draw the lines decides how many seats each party wins.

intro_slides.body: The west is Ken country, where Sean Matsuda runs strong. The city core leans Ryu behind Sakura. And out east, along the Bend, the Chun-Li Party takes about two in five — ahead of both the others on its home ground.
intro_slides.heading: A Three-Cornered Race

intro_slides.body: Each party has one part of the Bend. Draw a district around each base — west, city, east — and all three can carry a seat. Blur those lines and one base swallows another; split the east across districts and Chun-Li's two-in-five becomes a plurality nowhere.
intro_slides.heading: Three Bases, Three Corners

intro_slides.body: Hawthorn city is where most people live. Carve three equal-width columns and the middle one bursts the balance limit. Like your last legal map, the crowded centre needs the SMALLER district — draw it narrow, and let the rural wings run wide.
intro_slides.heading: The Dense Centre Needs Less Land

narrative.objective: Draw three balanced, connected districts — a legal map, like before — and read the result. There's no seat to chase: the winners emerge from where you put the lines. Keep the eastern base whole and Chun-Li carries that seat; split it across districts and she's shut out — repaint and watch the three-cornered race shift.
narrative.epilogue: A third party changes the map. A party with a concentrated base is powerful when its ground stays together and powerless when it's split — the same packing-and-cracking that moves seats between two sides, now with three. And the crowded city taught the other half of the lesson: dense ground needs the smaller district, so the centre is drawn tight and the rural wings run wide. The lines don't just pick between two sides — they decide how many corners keep a seat.
